 Sandia model makes asteroid-deflection simulations more than 1,600 times faster
 Tuesday, 3 November 2026, 20:12 
 Photo source: The Register 
 A combined simulation model can handle irregular asteroid shapes while reducing calculation time. Simulations found that changing which side of an asteroid faces an X-ray blast can produce up to a fivefold difference in its velocity change. 
 Researchers at Sandia National Laboratories, led by staff physicist Nathan Moore, developed a method to model how X-rays from a nuclear detonation near an asteroid could change its trajectory. Their findings were described in a recently published research paper.
 This is reported by The Register .
 Earlier calculations took so long that researchers often had to model asteroids as spheres or simplify the physics. Moore’s team combined two simulation codes already used at Sandia: ALEGRA, which models radiation heating and high-energy material dynamics, and SPARTA, which simulates low-density gases.
 “ALEGRA … can very accurately simulate the vaporization of the rocky surface, but the calculation becomes more inefficient for matter at low densities,” 
 – Nathan Moore
 In the combined model, ALEGRA handles regions of high gas density, while SPARTA models more dilute regions. Moore said in a Sandia press release that the approach is more than 1,600 times faster than earlier methods while retaining sufficient accuracy to predict deflection of irregularly shaped asteroids.
 Advertisement 
 Simulations of three well-studied asteroids – Golevka, Bennu and Itokawa – found that directing X-rays at different sides of the same asteroid could produce up to a fivefold difference in the resulting velocity change. Bennu, the most symmetrical of the three, still showed nearly twofold differences depending on which side faced the blast.
 “We expected aim to matter,” Moore said. “What surprised us was how much.” 
 – Nathan Moore
 The paper notes that an incoming asteroid may be poorly understood, and there may not be enough time to study it before attempting deflection. The team also said that predicting the outcome accurately is difficult without knowing an asteroid’s composition and internal structure, and its orientation may not be known.
